title: AI policy generator: what should your company's AI use policy say?
description: Free AI policy generator and template: answer 10 questions and get an editable AI use policy for your industry, data and locations.
verdict: Most staff already use AI at work, and nearly half have put company information into public tools.[^1][^4]
Bans backfire: misuse was highest where AI was banned, so write rules for using approved tools well.[^4][^5]
The rules that matter most are which tools, what data goes in, who approves, and who reviews output.[^6][^16]
Hiring, lending, insurance and health decisions carry extra legal rules; the generator adds those clauses only where they apply.[^11][^13]

steps: Answer 10 plain questions about your industry, size, data, AI tools, people decisions and locations.
Read your full policy on the page, with the three things to fix next. Edit any line directly.
See which of your AI uses are high risk and what control the policy adds, then check any other use.
Copy it, download it for Word or as Markdown, or print it.
method: Every policy has 18 sections: scope, owner, approved tools, data rules, human review, training, incidents and yearly review.[^6][^7]
Answers switch clauses on. Health data adds the business associate rule, credit adds adverse-action reasons, and clinical AI adds the Section 1557 check.[^12][^13][^22]
State, city and EU clauses come from the law's text or the regulator's own page, checked on 26 Nov 2026.[^10][^11]
The risk check sorts each AI use into Low, Medium, High or Not allowed, following the EU AI Act's risk levels and NIST.[^9][^7]
Defaults we chose ourselves are marked Zavient estimate: a 5-day answer on tool requests and 24-hour incident reports.[^7]

summary: An AI use policy tells staff which AI tools they can use, what information may go in, and who checks the output.[^6][^7] This generator builds yours from 10 questions, adding clauses for your industry, data and locations. It's a starting draft for your adviser, not legal advice.
humanRole: Your COO or head of operations owns the policy and names who approves new AI tools.[^7][^19]
A qualified person reviews AI output before it reaches customers, regulators or the public.[^6][^1]
People make every decision about someone's job, credit, insurance or care; AI only prepares the information.[^14][^18]
Your legal or compliance adviser reviews the draft before you adopt it, because state and EU rules keep changing.[^10][^9]

faq.q: Is there a free AI policy template we can use?
faq.a: Yes. This generator is free, needs no email, and builds a full AI use policy from your answers. You edit it instead of adapting a fixed template.[^6][^15]

faq.q: Should we ban ChatGPT at work?
faq.a: Usually not. In one global study, policy-breaking AI use was most common where AI was banned, so approved tools plus clear rules work better.[^4][^5]

faq.q: What should an AI acceptable use policy include?
faq.a: Scope, an owner, approved tools, a rule for each kind of data, human review, approval for new tools, training, incident reporting and a yearly review.[^7][^16]

faq.q: Who should own the AI policy at a mid-size company?
faq.a: One named senior owner, often the COO, with input from IT, HR and legal. Larger firms often use a small working group instead.[^7][^19]

faq.q: Do we need an AI policy if we have EU staff or customers?
faq.a: The EU AI Act asks deployers to take steps to build staff AI literacy, supervised nationally from 2 August 2026. A written policy with a training record helps show you did.[^8][^9]

faq.q: Do we need separate rules for AI in hiring?
faq.a: Hiring AI carries extra duties. New York City requires a bias audit within a year of use, and federal anti-discrimination law still applies to AI-assisted decisions.[^11][^14]

faq.q: How often should we update our AI policy?
faq.a: At least every 12 months, and sooner when a law, a major tool or an incident changes things. Colorado rewrote its AI law in 2026, for example.[^7][^10]

pickElse: You are a broker-dealer using AI in client communications → start from FINRA's notice and your supervisory procedures, then use this draft for staff use.[^20]
You are an insurer → also write the AI program the NAIC model bulletin describes; this policy covers how staff use AI.[^21]
You use AI in clinical decisions → also review each tool's inputs under Section 1557; the generator adds the clause, not the review.[^22]
You want a certified AI management system → use ISO 42001; an AI policy is one part of it.[^19]

reviews.notes: Wanted to know who owns it and how fast requests get answered. Owner and a 5-day default are in sections 3 and 10; an undecided owner becomes a fix-next item.
Needed it in Word for the handbook. Added Download for Word and Markdown, and yellow marks for the gaps to fill.
Worried it would read as a ban. Section 1 and the encouraged-uses list lead with using AI well; people stay in charge.
Asked whether their team's AI use needs sign-off. Added the risk summary from the answers, with the control for each high-risk use, plus the per-use check.
Asked what legal exposure is left. Fix-next lists legal items first; the disclaimer and law date sit at the top and in the policy footer.
